Using the information in the table above, we will compute the following statistics:


\(\textbf{Part A}\)

(a) Mean \( \displaystyle \bar{x}=\frac{\sum{fX}}{\sum{f}}=\frac{{@sum_fxi@}}{{@n@}}={@mean@}\)

(b) Median

The median class is that class containing the \( \displaystyle \left( \frac{{@total_f@}}{2}\right)\) item \(={@median_cf@}^{\text{th}}\)item.

Therefore, the median class is \({@float(lower_bound)@}-{@float(upper_bound)@}\).

Thus \(B_L={@float(lower_bound)@}, \, \displaystyle \left( \frac{n}{2}\right)={@median_cf@}, \, f_c={@f_median@}, \, i={@float(upper_bound)@}-{@float(lower_bound)@}={@width@}, \, cf_b={@cf_lower@} \)

Therefore,

\( \begin{align} \displaystyle md &=B_L+ \left( \frac{\frac{N}{2}-cf_b}{f_c}\right) \cdot i \\ &={@float(lower_bound)@}+ \left( \frac{\frac{{@total_f@}}{2}-{@cf_lower@}}{{@f_median@}}\right) \cdot {@width@} \\ &={@float(lower_bound)@}+{@md1@} \\ &={@ta@} \end{align}\)

The median immunity percentage in home exposure is the value \({@ta@}\).

(c) Mode

When dealing with grouped data, the mode represents the value or values in a dataset that have the highest frequency.

To calculate the mode for our grouped data, we will use the following formula:

\(\displaystyle \text{Mode}=L+\left( \frac{f_1 - f_0}{(f_1 - f_0)+(f_1 - f_2)}\right )\cdot h\)

Where:

-\( L={@float(Lm)@}\): Lower boundary of the modal class (class with the highest frequency)

- \(f_1={@f1m@}\): Frequency of the modal class

- \(f_0={@f0m@}\): Frequency of the class preceding the modal class

- \(f_2={@f2m@}\): Frequency of the class succeeding the modal class

- \(h={@hm@}\): Class width (the difference between upper and lower boundaries of each class)

\(\displaystyle \text{Mode}={@float(Lm)@}+\left( \frac{{@f1m@}- {@f0m@}}{({@f1m@}- {@f0m@})+({@f1m@} - {@f2m@})}\right )\cdot {@hm@}={@Mode@}\)

This formula allows us to estimate the mode for grouped data by taking into account the relative frequencies of the modal class and its neighboring classes.

It's important to note that the mode for grouped data is an estimate and may not represent an exact value within the dataset.

(d) Standard deviation \( \displaystyle \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum{f(x-\bar{x})^2}}{\sum f}}= \sqrt{\frac{{@mean_squared_diffs@}}{{@n@}}}={@standard_deviation@}\)

(e) Variance \( \displaystyle { \sigma^2}=\frac{{@mean_squared_diffs@}}{{@n@}}={@variance@}\)


\(\textbf{Part B}\)

To calculate the moments, skewness, and kurtosis, we first need to find the central moment of the distribution. The central moment is given by the formula:

\(\displaystyle M_n = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^n \cdot f_i \)

Where:

  • \(M_n\) is the central moment of order \(n\).
  • \(N\) is the total number of data points (in this case, the sum of all frequencies).
  • \(x_i\) is the midpoint of each class interval.
  • \(\bar{x}\) is the assumed mean ({@mean@} in this case).
  • \(n\) is the order of the moment.
  • \(f_i\) is the frequency of the class interval.

Let's calculate the moments, skewness, and moment coefficient of kurtosis for the given data:

  • Calculate the central moments:

    \( \displaystyle \begin{align} (a)\, M_2 &= \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{5} (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \cdot f_i \\ &=\frac{{@mean_squared_diffs@}}{{@n@}} \\ &={@decimalplaces(M2,2)@} \\ \\ (b)\, M_3 &= \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{5} (x_i - \bar{x})^3 \cdot f_i \\ &=\frac{{@sum_m3@}}{{@n@}} \\ &={@decimalplaces(M3,2)@} \\ \\ (c)\, M_4 &= \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{5} (x_i - \bar{x})^4 \cdot f_i \\ &=\frac{{@sum_m4@}}{{@n@}} \\ &={@decimalplaces(M4,2)@} \end{align} \)

    • Now, you can calculate \(Sk\) and \(Ku\) using the values of \(M_2\), \(M_3\), and \(M_4\).

    (d) \( \displaystyle \text{Moment Coefficient of Skewness (Sk) } = \frac{M_3}{M_2^{\frac{3}{2}}}={@Sk@}\)

    (e) \(\displaystyle \text{Moment Coefficient of Kurtosis (Ku) } = \frac{M_4}{M_2^2} - 3={@Ku@}\)
